Taking the wheel also means accepting responsibility for your actions and protecting other road users. We then connect that responsibility with speed limits. A limit gives the maximum legal speed for ideal conditions; active school or work-zone signs and conditions that make that speed unsafe require a slower choice. These instructions belong together: the position tells you where your hands go, and the grip tells you how to hold the wheel. In a practice example, Lena notices she is using her palms. She changes to a finger-and-thumb grip while keeping her hands at eight and four. Construction or bad weather can also make the posted speed unsafe. The second is the safe speed: even a legal speed can be unsafe, and conditions can require you to slow below the sign. We will also look at the opposite problem, driving so slowly that you block the normal flow of traffic. Never pass a school bus while it loads or unloads. Flashing red signals and the extended stop sign both command a full stop. And the stop applies from either direction, unless a separation or median divides the road. So bus reds and the stop arm stop traffic from both directions, while a separation or median between the roadways releases the far side. Many drivers think that only the traffic behind the bus must stop, but on an undivided road, oncoming traffic must stop too. Only a separation or median between the roadways releases the far side.
